A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core framework, and retained results. Their text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable; v1 Appendices A–D correspond to v2 Appendices A–D, with Appendix E added.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original linear-regression simulations, including empirical risks averaged over 100 runs and comparisons with theoretical predictions in Figures 1–2.

after.justification: v2 retains the original simulations and adds empirical studies of dynamic mixing, reused labels, refreshed covariates, and pooled real/synthetic data in Figures 3–5.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Algorithms 2–4 introduce interpolation procedures that reuse original labels, refresh covariates each iteration, or fit concatenated real/synthetic datasets. Pooling replaces the original shared-covariate weighted-label update with a combined-data estimator. Algorithm 1 and the previously defined dynamic-weight recursion remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond fixed covariates with fresh labels to three distinct scenarios: reused original labels, independently refreshed covariates, and separate real/synthetic covariate batches with partial real-label availability. Figures 3(c), 4(b), and 5 evaluate these scenarios; the original synthetic regression coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Figure 3(b) adds an empirical comparison of dynamic weighting, fixed golden-ratio weighting, and real-only weighting w=1. v1's iteration plot evaluates fixed golden-ratio weighting, while dynamic mixing appears only in its theoretical analysis. No external benchmark method is added.

E3.justification: The original risk metric and Figures 1–2 settings are retained. Added simulations introduce configurations including n=500 and 50 iterations for reused labels, n=1500 and 20 iterations for refreshed covariates, and n=100 with 100 plotted iterations for pooled data. These are settings for new experiments, not revisions to the earlier runs.

E4.justification: v2 adds empirical fixed-versus-dynamic mixing analysis, optimal-weight sensitivity to aspect ratio, and tests of whether fresh labels and shared covariates are essential. Figures 3–5 substantially extend the analysis of applicability and failure conditions beyond v1's covariance, noise, and regularization studies.

E5.justification: The 100-run averaging information is retained for the original plots, now described as the 'first two plots.' No changed replication count is reported for matched experiments, and the added simulations introduce no run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 retain identical plot content. New findings include near-overlap of dynamic and fixed golden-ratio risks after two iterations, optimal w=1 when labels are reused, aspect-ratio-dependent optimal weights with refreshed covariates, and exponentially growing pooled-data risk at gamma=2.1, 2.2, and 2.5. These are additional outcomes under distinct conditions.

T1.justification: Theorems 5.1, E.1, and E.2 add risk characterizations, an optimal-weight formula, and a pooled-data divergence condition, with proofs in Appendix E. Remark E.1 specifies the different limit order for refreshed covariates. Existing proofs also receive corrections, including removal of the extra covariance factor in equation (C.3) and restoration of a factor of two in its base-case identity.

C1.justification: The abstract newly claims to characterize when collapse is inevitable and when synthetic data helps across three additional data-generation settings. This substantially broadens the contribution beyond v1's fresh-label, fixed-covariate framework, while retaining its golden-ratio and ridge-regression claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains that synthetic augmentation cannot improve the studied fixed-label procedure, that refreshed covariates make both bias and variance weight-dependent, and that pooling can produce collapse despite fresh real labels. These findings materially qualify the applicability of the original collapse-prevention conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 documents the added simulations' sample sizes, iteration counts, SNRs, and covariate-generation assumptions—for example, n=1500, SNR=5, and 20 iterations in Figure 4(b). Existing experimental details are retained; no code-release, hardware, or runtime information is added.

R1.justification: v2 adds Li et al. (2021), Gneiting et al. (2005), and Rezaei et al. (2025), supporting label-reuse motivation and synthetic-data positioning. Its introduction broadens the description of He et al. (2025) from Gaussian ordinary least squares to low-dimensional GLMs and nonparametric estimation, although the abstract retains the narrower description.

P1.justification: The introduction gains motivation and related-work explanations, some theorem statements are streamlined, and Section 5 plus Appendix E are inserted. Most existing exposition and section order remain intact. The expanded introduction also contains two substantially duplicated motivation paragraphs.

P2.justification: Figures 3–5 add substantial visual evidence on mixing dynamics, aspect-ratio sensitivity, label reuse, and collapse; Algorithms 2–4 add corresponding procedure displays. Figures 1–2 preserve their plot content but move with the document reflow and receive edited captions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially clarifies how collapse prevention depends on data-refresh assumptions, an important boundary left unexplored in v1. Section 5 and Appendix E supply theoretical results and supporting simulations showing when synthetic augmentation helps, fails to help, or causes collapse; existing algebraic corrections also improve reliability. These gains outweigh the duplicated introductory text, inconsistent prior-work wording, and unspecified replication counts for the new simulations.
